title: What the Bible Says About the Poor and the Stranger
excerpt: Scripture returns to the poor and the stranger hundreds of times, across law and prophets and Gospels, and the church has learned to read past every one of them.
body:
A man sleeps under the overpass two blocks from our church. I have driven past him on my way to preach about him. That is not a confession I enjoy making, but it is the truest sentence I can write to begin, because the question of what the Bible says about the poor is never first a question of exegesis. It is a question of who we have trained ourselves not to see. The text was never the problem. We were.

## The Question Beneath the Exegesis

The real question is not whether Scripture cares about the poor. Even the most casual reader knows it does. The real question is why a book so relentless on this subject has produced a church so comfortable with poverty. Hundreds of passages across the law and the prophets and the Gospels touch wealth and want, the orphan and the widow, the laborer and the gleaner. We have read them and built sanctuaries with good parking. Something in us has learned to receive these texts as decoration rather than command.

> The text was never the problem. We were.

The strongest objection deserves a fair hearing, because it is not stupid and it is not made only by the hard of heart. It runs like this. The biblical commands about the poor were given to a covenant nation, ancient Israel, a theocracy with specific agrarian laws for a specific people in a specific land. Gleaning laws assume fields. Jubilee assumes tribal allotment. The year of release assumes a shared bloodline. To lift these statutes out of Iron Age Canaan and drop them onto a modern pluralistic economy is, the argument goes, a category mistake. And the political reading of these texts has often been lazy, baptizing whatever policy the reader already preferred. That critique lands. The Bible is not a budget proposal, and people who quote Leviticus to win an election usually have not read Leviticus.

## The Strongest Objection: Laws for a Covenant Nation

But here the strong objection breaks on a single word, and the word is ger. The sojourner. The stranger. The resident alien who belonged to no tribe, held no allotment, and stood outside the bloodline entirely. If the poverty laws were merely tribal housekeeping, the ger should have been excluded from them by definition. He is the one person the covenant could have ignored without contradiction. Instead he is named again and again, woven into the very statutes the objection says were for insiders only. 'When you reap the harvest of your land, you shall not reap your field right up to its edge, neither shall you gather the gleanings after your harvest. You shall leave them for the poor and for the sojourner' (Leviticus 23:22 ESV). The stranger gleans the same field as the widow. The law reaches past the boundary it supposedly defends.

## The Stranger Who Breaks the Argument

This is the text I want to carry, because the ger exposes the engine underneath the whole code. Why include the outsider. The answer is given without argument, as a brute fact of Israel's identity. 'You shall love the sojourner, for you were sojourners in the land of Egypt' (Deuteronomy 10:19 ESV). The memory of slavery is the foundation of mercy. Israel is commanded to treat the vulnerable as it wished it had been treated when it was vulnerable, when it had no land, no rights, no name worth recording in Pharaoh's ledgers. The poverty laws are not tribal property management. They are the moral residue of a rescue. A redeemed people remembers the pit.

The Hebrew has a word for the whole class of the unprotected, the anawim. The bowed-down ones. Abraham Heschel, reading the prophets, saw that their fury was never abstract. 'The prophet's word is a scream in the night,' he wrote, and while the world lies at ease and asleep, the prophet feels the blast from heaven (Heschel 1962). Amos does not condemn Israel for theological error in the seminary sense. He condemns men who 'trample the head of the poor into the dust of the earth' (Amos 2:7 ESV), who sell the righteous for silver and the needy for a pair of sandals. Isaiah indicts a worship that runs perfectly while the orphan goes uncared for, fasts that God refuses to smell because the fast he chose was 'to share your bread with the hungry and bring the homeless poor into your house' (Isaiah 58:7 ESV). The prophets did not separate the altar from the street. We did. That separation is our invention, not theirs.

## The Prophets Who Refused to Divide Altar From Street

> The prophets did not separate the altar from the street. We did.

Trace the historical root and the picture sharpens uncomfortably. The early church took these texts at face value in ways that scandalized Rome. By the fourth century the emperor Julian, who hated Christianity and tried to roll it back, complained in a letter around 362 that the 'impious Galileans support not only their own poor but ours as well.' The pagan world noticed Christians feeding strangers who were not theirs. Then came Constantine, then came land, then came endowment, and slowly the church that had been a refuge for the ger became a property owner with the ger outside its gates. The Reformers fought over grace and missed the poor. The American church, born in a land of seemingly endless property, baptized acquisition as blessing and read the poverty texts as metaphors for spiritual lack. We spiritualized hunger so we would not have to feed it. I have preached that sermon. I am inside this.

## How the Church Learned to Spiritualize Hunger

And here the reversal, because the gospel does not leave the comfortable reader where it found him. We imagine ourselves the gleaners, the generous ones with full fields choosing to leave a corner. Scripture will not let us keep that seat. The whole arc of redemption casts us not as the landowner but as the ger, the stranger with no claim, the bowed-down one who was 'alienated from the commonwealth of Israel and strangers to the covenants of promise, having no hope and without God in the world' (Ephesians 2:12 ESV). We are the sojourner. We did not earn our place at the table. It was given to us by a God who remembered our slavery when we had forgotten it ourselves.

This is where the cross does the argument's real work, and not as sentiment. The law demanded the gleaning, the open hand, the remembered pit, and we did not keep it. We reaped to the edges. We trampled heads into dust. The law's verdict on us is just, and it is severe, and we cannot answer it. So Christ became poor. 'For your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich' (2 Corinthians 8:9 ESV). He took the position of the anawim absolutely, naked on a Roman beam, executed outside the city wall where the unclean and the foreign were thrown. The one with every claim took the place of the one with none. Mercy to the poor is not a moral upgrade we add to faith. It is the faith, worked outward, because we have received exactly the mercy the poverty laws describe. We give what we were given. To withhold it is to forget Egypt.

## The Cross and the Poverty of Christ

The man under the overpass is still there tonight. I know his approximate location and not his name. The Bible says what it says about the poor and the stranger, with a clarity that does not require a scholar to decode, and the distance between that clarity and my life is not a gap in my theology. It is the gap. Heschel said the prophet's task was to make us feel the scream we had learned to sleep through. The text has done its work. The field still has corners.

> We give what we were given. To withhold it is to forget Egypt.

We were sojourners in the land of Egypt. We are not allowed to forget it.

### Works Cited

Heschel, Abraham J. The Prophets. New York: Harper and Row, 1962.

The Holy Bible, English Standard Version. Wheaton: Crossway, 2001.

title: Disability, Dignity, and the Image of God
excerpt: A theology that locates human worth in capacity will eventually run out of people it can call human.
body:
There is a moment in many churches when a man with a profound intellectual disability is wheeled in, and the room does not know where to put its eyes. I have been the pastor in that room. I have felt the congregation's discomfort and my own, the polite warmth that is really a wish for the moment to pass. We did not know what to do with him because we had quietly decided, without ever saying it, that worship is a thing you perform with a functioning mind. He could not perform it. So we wondered, in a place we would never admit to, whether he fully belonged. That wondering is the subject of this essay, and the answer to it indicts me first.

## Where Does Worth Come From

The real question underneath disability theology is not how to be kinder to disabled people. Kindness is cheap and condescending and the disabled have had enough of it. The real question is what makes a human being a human being. Where does worth come from. If we get that wrong, every act of inclusion is just charity extended from the strong to the weak, a favor that could be withdrawn. If we get it right, the whole arrangement reverses.

## The Secular Account of Dignity as Capacity

The strongest secular account deserves to be stated at full strength, because it is coherent and many thoughtful people hold it. Human dignity, on this view, is grounded in capacities. Reason, self-awareness, the ability to form preferences and projects and relationships, to suffer and anticipate and choose. The philosopher Peter Singer has argued this with a consistency most of us lack the nerve for, concluding that a being without these capacities does not have the moral status we grant to those who do. The strength of this position is that it takes the moral question seriously and refuses sentimental evasion. It also rightly insists that disabled people are not lesser, because most can reason and choose. As far as it goes it defends them. But notice the cost. It defends them by certifying their capacities. The dignity is real but it is earned, and what is earned by capacity can be lost by capacity. The man in the wheelchair fails the test.

## The Image That Cannot Be Earned or Lost

This is exactly where the Christian account does not merely soften the secular one. It overturns its foundation. And the overturning rests on a single text from the first page of Scripture. 'So God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him' (Genesis 1:27 ESV). The imago dei. Read carefully what it does not say. It does not say God created man with certain capacities and therefore in his image. The image is not a property we possess, like intelligence or speech or mobility, that could be measured and found lacking. The image is a status conferred by God in the act of creation, before the human being does anything at all. Worth is not earned by what the person can do. It is bestowed by whose the person is. The infant has it whole. The man with dementia has it whole. The child who will never speak a word has it whole, and intact, and undiminished by a single missing function.

> Worth is not earned by what the person can do. It is bestowed by whose the person is.

John Swinton, who has spent his life on this question, puts it with care that has cost him something. He argues that we have made human identity a matter of memory and cognition, so that when those fade we treat the person as fading too. But 'we are held in the memory of God,' Swinton writes, and that holding does not weaken when ours does (Swinton 2012). The person with advanced Alzheimer's who cannot remember his own name is remembered entirely by God, and that divine remembering, not his neural function, is what secures who he is. Stanley Hauerwas pressed the same nerve for decades, arguing that the church does not include the disabled as an act of generosity. The church learns from them what it could learn nowhere else, that none of us is self-sufficient, that dependence is not the human failure but the human condition, that we are all, every one of us, sustained by a love we did not generate.

## Henri Nouwen and the Man He Was Sent to Wash

Here the witness of Henri Nouwen does real work, because he did not theorize this. He lived it. Nouwen had been a professor at Harvard and Yale, a celebrated writer near the summit of the religious intellectual world. In 1986 he left it to join L'Arche Daybreak, a community where people with and without intellectual disabilities share life, and he was assigned to care for a man named Adam Arnett, who could not speak, could not walk unaided, could not feed or dress himself, and suffered frequent seizures. Nouwen bathed him, dressed him, fed him each morning. And the great spiritual writer of his generation came to call this man his teacher and his friend. Adam taught him, Nouwen wrote, that the heart of the person is not in the mind. 'Adam was the most vulnerable person I had ever known,' he wrote, 'and through his vulnerability he became my spiritual guide' (Nouwen 1997). The professor learned the gospel from the man he was sent to wash.

## The History the Church Would Rather Not Read

Trace the history and you find the church has not always been faithful here, which is why none of us gets to be smug. In 1939 Nazi Germany began the program later called Aktion T4, the systematic murder of disabled adults and children deemed lebensunwertes Leben, life unworthy of life. By 1941 it had killed more than seventy thousand people, and it ran with the cooperation of doctors and the silence of much of the church. There were exceptions. Bishop Clemens von Galen preached against it openly in 1941 at real risk to his life. But the broad silence was the scandal, and it grew from a soil the church had helped till, a long Christian habit of measuring souls by their usefulness, valuing the strong contributor and pitying the dependent. We had been speaking the language of capacity for centuries before the Nazis weaponized it. I do not get to read that history from a safe distance. The discomfort in my own sanctuary is the same root, smaller and quieter, but the same.

> We had been speaking the language of capacity for centuries before the Nazis weaponized it.

And now the reversal that the whole gospel turns on. We assume the disabled are the ones who need our help to reach God. Scripture says God reached us through weakness, deliberately, scandalously, on purpose. 'God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong,' Paul writes, 'God chose what is low and despised in the world, even things that are not, to bring to nothing things that are' (1 Corinthians 1:27, 28 ESV). The kingdom does not run on the currency of capacity. It runs on the opposite. The strong are not the patrons of the weak. The weak are the place God has chosen to dwell.

## The Cross as the Glory of Dependence

The cross seals this and will not let it become mere uplift. Christ in his passion was reduced to total dependence. He could not carry his own beam. He was stripped, immobilized, given vinegar by other hands, unable to wipe his own face or wave away the flies. Kelly Kapic notes that we instinctively read this as the interruption of his glory, the low point before the resurrection rescues him. But the cross is not the interruption of the glory. It is the glory (Kapic 2017). God reveals himself most fully not in a display of capacity but in an act of utter vulnerability, the imago dei shown in a body that could do nothing for itself. Which means the man we wheeled into the back of the sanctuary, the man we did not know where to seat, may be closer to the image of the crucified Christ than the able-bodied pastor at the pulpit who was so worried about the awkwardness. He was not the problem in that room. I was.

> Worth is not a wage. It is a gift, given by God in the making, and it cannot be earned and so it cannot be lost.

Worth is not a wage. It is a gift, given by God in the making, and it cannot be earned and so it cannot be lost. The man in the wheelchair bears the image whole. He always did. The question was never whether he belonged among us.

The question was whether we could bear to belong to a God who looks like him.

### Works Cited

Kapic, Kelly M. Embodied Hope: A Theological Meditation on Pain and Suffering. Downers Grove: IVP Academic, 2017.

Nouwen, Henri J. M. Adam: God's Beloved. Maryknoll: Orbis Books, 1997.

Swinton, John. Dementia: Living in the Memories of God. Grand Rapids: Eerdmans, 2012.

The Holy Bible, English Standard Version. Wheaton: Crossway, 2001.

title: Mental Health and the Church: Beyond Just Pray About It
excerpt: A church that treats depression as a faith problem will keep handing the drowning a heavier stone.
body:
A woman sat across from me in my office and told me she had stopped wanting to be alive. She had told her small group the week before and been advised to pray more and trust God. She had been praying. She had been trusting God for eleven years through a depression that the praying had not lifted, and the advice had landed on her not as comfort but as verdict, one more proof that her suffering was a measure of her failing faith. She left that group. She nearly left the church. She nearly left more than that. I have replayed that conversation many times, because the counsel she received was not malicious. It was sincere, and it was lethal, and some version of it has come out of my own mouth.

## What the Church Believes Suffering Is

The real question is not whether Christians should care about mental health. Of course they should, and most will say so. The real question is what the church believes mental suffering is. Underneath the counsel to 'just pray about it' lies a theology, usually unexamined, that the mind is the seat of the spirit and that a sick mind is therefore a sick soul. Get that theology wrong and every kind word becomes an accusation. The depressed hear that their condition is a sin to repent of. The anxious hear that their fear is a failure to believe. We hand the drowning a heavier stone and call it encouragement.

## The Objection That Guards Something True

> We hand the drowning a heavier stone and call it encouragement.

The strongest form of the objection is worth stating fairly, because it is not pure ignorance and it guards something true. It runs this way. The Bible promises peace that surpasses understanding. It commands us not to be anxious. It says the joy of the Lord is our strength. To rush a suffering believer to a psychiatrist, the concern goes, is to treat as medical what is finally spiritual, to medicate away a soul's true ache, to let the culture redefine sin as illness and conviction as a chemical imbalance. There is a real danger there. Our age does sometimes flatten the moral into the clinical, calling a thing a disorder so no one has to call it anything harder. A church that simply outsourced every inner struggle to medication would have abandoned its calling. That much is right.

## Elijah Under the Broom Tree

But the strong objection collapses on a single body, and the body is the prophet Elijah. Carry his story as the spine, because Scripture refuses to spiritualize him. In 1 Kings 19, immediately after the greatest victory of his ministry on Mount Carmel, Elijah runs into the wilderness, sits under a broom tree, and prays to die. 'It is enough,' he says, 'now, O Lord, take away my life' (1 Kings 19:4 ESV). Here is a man of titanic faith, fresh off calling down fire from heaven, in the grip of what any honest reader recognizes as suicidal despair. Now watch what God does, because it is the whole sermon. God does not rebuke him. God does not tell him to pray more or trust harder or claim a promise. God lets him sleep. Then an angel wakes him and feeds him. Then lets him sleep again, and feeds him again. 'And he lay down and slept under a broom tree. And behold, an angel touched him and said to him, Arise and eat' (1 Kings 19:5 ESV). Before a single word of theology, God addresses Elijah's body. Rest. Food. Then more rest, more food. Only after the body is tended does the quiet voice come, and even then it does not scold. The divine response to a faithful man's collapse is not a lecture. It is sleep and bread.

> The divine response to a faithful man's collapse is not a lecture. It is sleep and bread.

This is the text the church has skipped. We have read Elijah as a hero and refused to read him as a sufferer, because a depressed prophet complicates a theology that needs faith and despair to be opposites. They are not. Curt Thompson, a psychiatrist who works at the intersection of faith and the brain, names the mechanism the church most often ignores. Shame. Shame works by isolation, he argues, driving us into hiding precisely from the community and vulnerability that would heal it, the very things we need most (Thompson 2015). The suffering believer who is told her depression is a faith deficiency is driven into hiding by shame, away from the one community that might hold her, deeper into the isolation that feeds the illness. The very counsel meant to help operates the engine that destroys. Elijah's God did the opposite. He came to Elijah in his hiding place and fed him there.

## The Mechanism of Shame and Isolation

Trace the history and the wound is partly our own making. For most of Christian history the care of the soul and the care of the mind were not split. The monastic tradition knew acedia, the noonday demon, a paralyzing heaviness the desert fathers treated with rhythm, labor, and community, not condemnation. Then came the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, the rise of modern medicine, and a hard fork. The body and mind went to the doctors. The soul went to the clergy. Each side guarded its territory and grew suspicious of the other, and the church, having ceded the brain to medicine, was left preaching to a self it no longer believed was embodied. By the twentieth century much of American evangelicalism treated psychology as a rival gospel, antidepressants as a crutch for the faithless, the counselor's office as a place real Christians did not need. We built that wall. I was handed it already built and I reinforced it before I knew what it was.

## How the Care of Soul and Mind Were Split

Here the reversal the gospel always brings. We assume strong faith means the absence of anguish, that the mature believer has moved past the dark places. Scripture gives us a Savior in a garden, sweating, begging, asking that the cup pass, 'sorrowful, even to death' (Matthew 26:38 ESV). The most faithful human being who ever lived experienced anguish so severe that Luke, a physician, records his sweat falling like drops of blood. Mental and emotional torment is not the opposite of faith. It sat in the soul of the Son of God on the worst night of human history. The presence of anguish proves nothing about the absence of faith. The garden settles that forever.

## The Garden That Settles the Question

And the cross does the deepest work, against the lie underneath all the bad counsel. The lie is that suffering this severe must be punishment, that the depressed are reaping what their weak faith has sown, that affliction is the wage of some hidden sin. The cross detonates that arithmetic. There the only truly innocent man bore the most extreme anguish, body and mind and spirit, and bore it precisely because suffering is not a clean ledger of personal fault. Kelly Kapic writes that the cross frees us from the cruelty of believing our pain is always our own doing (Kapic 2017). Christ cried out that he was forsaken. If forsakenness can pass through the soul of the sinless one, then the darkness in the soul of a suffering saint is not the proof of God's absence. It may be the very place he is nearest, with bread, the way he came to Elijah.

The woman in my office did not need a heavier stone. She needed what the angel brought the prophet under the broom tree. Rest. Food. A presence that did not flinch from her despair or assign it a moral grade. She needed the church to stop preaching at her drowning and to get in the water. We have the resources for this, the medicine and the counselors and the doctors God has given, and we have the deeper resource, a God who feeds the despairing before he teaches them.

> Pray about it. Yes. And then bring the bread.

Pray about it. Yes. And then bring the bread.

### Works Cited

Kapic, Kelly M. Embodied Hope: A Theological Meditation on Pain and Suffering. Downers Grove: IVP Academic, 2017.

Thompson, Curt. The Soul of Shame: Retelling the Stories We Believe About Ourselves. Downers Grove: IVP Books, 2015.

The Holy Bible, English Standard Version. Wheaton: Crossway, 2001.

title: What the Bible Says About Immigrants and Refugees
excerpt: Scripture commands love of the foreigner not as policy but as memory, and a people who forget the pit will always fear the stranger.
body:
I grew up without a father, which means I grew up knowing what it is to belong somewhere only conditionally. Not a stranger in a foreign country, nothing so severe. But close enough to the experience of standing at an edge, watching a household you are not quite inside, to make me suspicious of how easily settled people talk about who belongs. That suspicion is the only credential I bring to this subject. The Bible says a great deal about immigrants and refugees, and most of what it says is aimed precisely at people like the man I have become, comfortable, established, holding the keys to a house I did not build.

## The Question Prior to Policy

The real question is not whether Christians may hold views on immigration policy. They may, and faithful believers land in different places on enforcement and borders and law, and anyone who tells you Scripture dictates a particular statute is selling something. The real question is prior to policy and deeper than it. How does God regard the foreigner. What is the disposition of his heart toward the one who arrives with nothing, and what does he command of the people who claim his name. Settle that, and the policy arguments become arguments among people who have first agreed on what the stranger is worth.

## The Objection That Guards Law and Duty

The strongest objection is serious and I will not caricature it. It runs like this. The biblical commands about the ger, the resident alien, were given to ancient Israel about the legal sojourner, the one who entered the land lawfully and submitted to its covenant and its statutes. The ger was a documented resident, the argument goes, not a category that maps onto unlawful entry, and to flatten every distinction between the lawful immigrant and the unlawful is to misuse the text. Furthermore, the argument continues, Romans 13 establishes the legitimate authority of the governing power to maintain order and enforce law, and a nation has a real obligation to its own citizens, the duty of a household to its own. This is not a frivolous position. It guards two true things. Law matters, and a government does owe primary duties to those in its care. A serious reading of Scripture cannot wave those away.

## How Much the Law Granted the Stranger

But the strong objection runs into the wall of how much the law actually granted the ger, and the wall is high. Carry one text as the spine, the same one that exposed the engine of the whole code. 'You shall not wrong a sojourner or oppress him, for you were sojourners in the land of Egypt' (Exodus 22:21 ESV). Notice the ground given. Not the sojourner's legal paperwork. Not his usefulness to the economy. The memory of Israel's own time as foreigners under Pharaoh. And notice how far the protection extends. The ger was to receive the same justice in court as the native born, the same sabbath rest, the gleanings of the field, a share in the festivals, even inclusion in the cities of refuge. 'You shall have the same rule for the sojourner and for the native, for I am the Lord your God' (Leviticus 24:22 ESV). The objection wants to limit the ger to the carefully documented. The law itself extends to him a near-equality the modern settled citizen would find radical if it were proposed today.

> He is partisan toward them, and a people who claim him and fear them have not understood whom they worship.

And the deeper answer reaches past statute into the marrow of who God says he is. 'He executes justice for the fatherless and the widow, and loves the sojourner, giving him food and clothing' (Deuteronomy 10:18 ESV). God does not merely permit the foreigner. He loves him, and feeds him, and the command to Israel is to imitate that love because they were objects of it first. Abraham Heschel saw that this was the prophetic nerve, that God's concern for the powerless was not one attribute among many but the revelation of his character. The greatness of a prophet, as Heschel described it, lay in the capacity to hold God and humanity together in a single thought, pleading for God before the people and for the people before God (Heschel 1962). The God of the prophets is not neutral toward the displaced. He is partisan toward them, and a people who claim him and fear them have not understood whom they worship.

## A Scripture Written by Refugees

Trace the history and Scripture turns out to be a record of refugees from beginning to end. Abraham was a wanderer who left Ur for a land not yet his. Jacob's family came to Egypt as economic migrants fleeing famine. The whole nation was born as a column of refugees walking out of slavery into a wilderness. Ruth was a Moabite immigrant, a foreigner of a despised people, who gleaned in Boaz's field under the very poverty laws written for the ger, and from that foreign woman came the line of David and the line of the Messiah. And the Messiah himself. Within two years of his birth, Matthew records, Joseph took the child and his mother and fled by night across a border into Egypt, escaping a king who meant to kill him. 'Rise, take the child and his mother, and flee to Egypt' (Matthew 2:13 ESV). The Son of God was a refugee child in a foreign land before he was anything else the world would later call him. The church that fears the refugee fears the infant it claims to follow.

## The Reversal the Comfortable Reader Must Feel

> Every Christian is a naturalized foreigner. We hold our place by grace and not by right.

Here is where the comfortable reader, and I am one, must feel the reversal. We instinctively cast ourselves as the settled householders deciding, from a position of ownership, whom to admit. We are the citizens. They are the strangers at the gate. Scripture takes that self-understanding and inverts it without apology. 'You are no longer strangers and aliens, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God' (Ephesians 2:19 ESV). The word translated stranger and alien is the language of immigration. Before grace, we were the undocumented ones, with no standing in the commonwealth of God, no claim on the household, no right of entry. We did not earn citizenship in the kingdom. It was extended to us as pure amnesty, a status conferred on aliens who had no legal basis to demand it. Every Christian is a naturalized foreigner. We hold our place by grace and not by right.

## The Amnesty Purchased Outside the Gate

The cross is where that amnesty was purchased, and it does the argument's hardest work. The law of the kingdom is exacting. None of us met its terms for entry. We arrived at its border with nothing, our papers a record of debt, no merit to present, no claim to make. The just verdict was exclusion, and it was deserved. Then Christ, the rightful Son, the one citizen with every claim, was himself cast outside the gate. 'So Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood' (Hebrews 13:12 ESV). He was expelled, executed beyond the wall in the place of the unclean and the foreign, so that the excluded could be brought in. He took the position of the deported one so the deportable could become citizens. This is not a metaphor we may admire and set aside. It is the ground of our standing. We are inside the household only because the Son was put outside it.

> A people who remember the pit do not get to fear the stranger.

Which leaves the settled Christian, leaves me, with a question that policy cannot answer and law cannot soften. The arguments about borders and enforcement are real, and I do not pretend the texts hand us a single statute. But underneath every such argument sits the prior thing, the disposition of the heart toward the one who arrives with nothing. And on that, Scripture is not ambiguous, and it is not gentle. We were sojourners. We were aliens with no claim, taken in by grace, given food and clothing and a place at a table we did not build. A people who remember the pit do not get to fear the stranger.

We loved him because he first loved us when we were the foreigners.

We are not permitted to forget the country we came from.

### Works Cited

Heschel, Abraham J. The Prophets. New York: Harper and Row, 1962.

The Holy Bible, English Standard Version. Wheaton: Crossway, 2001.

title: The Consistent Pro-Life Ethic: Womb to Tomb
excerpt: If life is sacred because it bears the image of God, then it is sacred at every point that image is borne, and our convenient exceptions are the tell.
body:
I have stood at both ends of a human life in one week. A hospital room where a couple held the hand of a man dying of cancer, and a different room where a young mother showed me the grainy image of the child she was carrying. Both rooms made the same demand on me, and I felt it as one demand, not two. This is a person. Do not look away. The trouble is that the church, and I have been part of this, has learned to feel that demand intensely in one room and faintly in another, depending on which end of life is in front of us and which political tribe owns the question. That selective feeling is the subject here, and the diagnosis is not comfortable.

## What We Mean by Pro-Life

The real question is not whether human life has value. Nearly everyone says it does. The real question is whether we mean it consistently, or whether 'pro-life' has shrunk into a single-issue slogan that lets us defend the unborn fiercely while we grow cold toward the prisoner, the refugee, the poor, the condemned, and the elderly who cost us time. A principle that applies only where it is convenient is not a principle. It is a preference wearing a principle's clothes.

## The Objection From the Uniquely Innocent

> A principle that applies only where it is convenient is not a principle. It is a preference wearing a principle's clothes.

The strongest objection comes from thoughtful people on more than one side, and it deserves a real hearing. From one direction it runs this way. The unborn child is uniquely innocent and uniquely defenseless, and to compare abortion to debates over capital punishment or immigration or welfare policy is to dilute the gravest injustice by burying it in a list, to trade the clear killing of the innocent for a fog of contested policy questions where reasonable people differ. That is a serious point and it guards something true. Not every life issue carries the same moral weight, and the deliberate ending of an innocent life is not equivalent to a disputed question of social policy. A consistent ethic that flattens every difference would be a moral failure of its own.

## The Image That Cannot Be Wielded Selectively

But the objection, taken at its strongest, actually drives toward the consistent ethic rather than away from it, and here is why. The argument for the unborn rests on a single foundation, that this small voiceless life bears the image of God and therefore may not be destroyed for our convenience. Take that foundation seriously and it does not stay put. Carry the text that grounds it. 'So God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him' (Genesis 1:27 ESV). The imago dei is the whole case for the unborn, and it is not a property that switches on at viability and off at conviction. It does not weaken with age or crime or citizenship or cost. If the image is what makes the child in the womb untouchable, then the image makes the man on death row untouchable, and the refugee at the border, and the prisoner, and the grandmother with dementia who no longer recognizes her children. The very principle that arms the defense of the unborn arms the defense of all of them. You cannot wield it selectively without cutting its edge off.

This is the argument the church has resisted, because consistency is expensive and tribal loyalty is cheap. The prophets had no such inconsistency. Their defense of life ran the full span of the vulnerable, the orphan and the widow and the poor and the foreigner, every category of the bowed-down ones, the anawim. Amos thundered against those who sold the needy for sandals. Isaiah condemned a nation whose hands were full of blood while it kept its festivals. Heschel, reading them, saw that their moral vision had no convenient exceptions. 'To us a single act of injustice is slight,' he wrote, 'to the prophets, a disaster' (Heschel 1962). A single act. Not a category we have prioritized. The prophets did not rank the vulnerable by political usefulness. Neither, it turns out, does the God they spoke for.

## The Early Church and the Whole Span of Life

> The prophets did not rank the vulnerable by political usefulness. Neither, it turns out, does the God they spoke for.

Trace the history and the early church holds up a mirror we would rather not look in. The Christians of the first centuries were known for refusing to take life at any point the surrounding culture took it casually. The Didache, a Christian text from around the late first century, commanded plainly, 'you shall not murder a child by abortion nor kill that which is born.' But the same Christians also defied Roman custom by rescuing infants left exposed to die, took in plague victims when pagans fled, and, in many witnesses, refused the spectacles of the arena where life was destroyed for entertainment. Their reverence did not begin and end at birth. It ran the whole span, womb to tomb, because their reverence was for the image and not for a faction's agenda. Somewhere across the centuries that consistency fractured, and in our own time it shattered along political lines, until one tribe defended the womb and abandoned the border and another defended the refugee and abandoned the womb, and both called the other a hypocrite, and both were right. I have lived inside that fracture. I have let my tribe tell me which deaths to grieve.

## The Reversal That Convicts the Defender

Here is the reversal the gospel forces on anyone honest enough to receive it. We like to imagine ourselves the defenders of life, the ones standing for the vulnerable against a careless world. Scripture asks a harder question. Whose blood is on our hands by the things we have left undone. 'Anyone who hates his brother is a murderer' (1 John 3:15 ESV). The line between the killer and the righteous defender is not as clean as our politics pretends. The God who knit the unborn child together also knit the prisoner we have stopped praying for and the enemy we have stopped seeing as human. The consistent ethic is not a burden laid on the pro-life cause from outside. It is the pro-life cause taken to its honest end, and it convicts me at the points where I had grown comfortable.

## The Cross Where No One Ranks the Vulnerable

The cross does the work no slogan can. There the sacredness of life and the cost of its destruction met in one body. Christ, who bore the image of God without flaw, was put to death by a coalition of the religious and the political, condemned by a legal process and executed by the state, the most innocent life ever lived destroyed for the convenience of those it threatened. The cross shows us with unbearable clarity what it is to take an image-bearing life, and it shows it to us as our own act, for it was our sin that nailed him there. We did this. And then the cross does the thing only grace can do. The God we murdered did not return for vengeance. He returned with forgiveness, and in that forgiveness exposed the cheapness of every ethic that defends some lives to feel righteous while discarding others to feel safe. At the foot of that cross no one gets to rank the vulnerable. We are all the killers, and we are all the ones for whom he died.

So the man in the hospital bed and the child on the grainy screen make one demand, and it is the same demand the convicted man makes from his cell and the mother makes at the border. This is a person. Do not look away. The image of God does not flicker on and off according to our convenience or our voting bloc. It is borne whole, at every point a human life is borne, from the first cell to the last breath.

> Womb to tomb. The whole span. No exceptions we get to keep.
